title: Micro-lattice fidelity and tool fallback PRD notes
content:
Context:
This doc captures a compact PRD sketch for an experiment we should run on progressive fidelity delivery and deterministic fallback behavior for tool calls inside streaming sessions. The goal is to give client SDKs a small set of primitives that let developers express how much progressive output they want, which parts can be truncated, and how to safe-fallback to non-tooling or lighter models when hosted capacity or tool latency spikes occur.

Problem statement:
- Many customers embed long-running streaming responses with optional tool invocations (search, run-code, DB lookups). When tool calls are slow or fail, the client experience is brittle: either the whole stream stalls or the client receives partial, non-actionable fragments.
- Current internal surfaces are optimized for full-response semantics (commit on tool results) or for optimistic, best-effort tool calls. Neither gives app developers a concise way to say: "stream partial narrative now, include tool output if it lands within X ms, otherwise synthesize a safe fallback summary."

User-facing goals (measurable):
1) Reduce end-to-end tail latency observed by mobile clients on sessions that use at least one tool by 25% in 95th percentile for targeted workloads.
2) Increase application-level continuity (sessions that show a usable result to user without manual retry) from 82% -> 95% for tool-augmented flows.
3) Provide SDKs with 3 ergonomic primitives that cover >90% of common fallback patterns used by pilot customers.

Non-goals:
- This is not a full rework of streaming protocol framing. Keep wire-protocol changes minimal and backwards-compatible.
- Not solving every tool orchestration problem (complex orchestrations remain domain of connectors/PS).

High-level approach: micro-lattice fidelity
- Introduce the micro-lattice as a client-declared fidelity lattice: an ordered list of progressively richer delivery tiers. Each tier describes output composition (narrative-only, narrative+metadata, narrative+tool-inline, narrative+tool-attachment).
- Server will attempt to satisfy the highest tier for each frame but can fall back to lower tiers deterministically based on policy (tool latency, capacity, model fallback, region).
- Client SDKs expose a small grammar to declare the lattice per-request or as a session default.

Core primitives (SDK ergonomics):
1) fidelity_lattice (list of tokens): an ordered list of named tiers developers pick from presets (e.g., fast, balanced, authoritative) or create ad-hoc.
2) tool_timeout_hint (ms): soft hint for how long server should wait for tool responses before emitting a lower-tier frame. Server treats this as a latency budget rather than a strict deadline.
3) attachment_mode: "inline" | "deferred" | "summarize-if-missing" — controls whether tool output should be interleaved, posted as an attachment event, or summarized if missing.

Example developer request snippet (pseudo):
- fidelity_lattice: ["narrative-only", "narrative+search-inline", "narrative+search-attachment"]
- tool_timeout_hint: 250
- attachment_mode: "summarize-if-missing"

Server behavior sketch:
- Streaming frames are annotated with tier names and a status flag: {tier: "narrative+search-inline", status: "fulfilled|fallback|degraded", reason: "tool-timeout|capacity|model-fallback"}.
- On tool invocation, we race between tool completion and the tool_timeout_hint. If tool returns before budget -> emit enriched frame at requested tier. If not, emit fallback frame built by synthesizing tool-summary or skipping the tool output (based on attachment_mode).
- If a fallback happens, server schedules a follow-up attachment event when/if the tool result later becomes available (unless attachment_mode == "inline-only").

Structured output and action semantics:
- Structured outputs (JSON/blobs) must include stable element ids so clients can reconcile fallback frames with later attachments. Example: {elements: [{id: "e1", type: "answer", content: "...", status: "fallback"}]}
- When tool output arrives later, a delta-attachment event will reference element ids and provide a replace/augment operation. Client SDKs should apply these deterministically.

Telemetry and observability:
- Emit per-request metrics: requested_lattice_depth, initial_tier_emitted, fallback_reason, tool_latency_ms, followup_attachment_count.
- Add an SLO dashboard for 'fallback rate' per model/tool combination and an alert if fallback_rate > 8% for production tenants.
- Trace-level examples should include snapshots of frames and status flags for postmortem and quality regression detection.

Operational policies and defaults:
- Default fidelity preset = ["narrative-only", "narrative+tool-attachment"] with tool_timeout_hint = 300ms and attachment_mode = "deferred".
- High-tier customers (Dedicated) get higher default budgets and can opt into optimistic inline attachments.
- Hosted control plane can define global thresholds that temporarily throttle inline-rich tiers during capacity pressure. These are surfaced in headers for client metrics.

Migration and backwards compatibility:
- If client does not supply fidelity_lattice, server behaves as today (best-effort, no deterministic tier tags).
- Introduce new lounge header X-RW-Fidelity: tier-name on frames — old clients will ignore unknown headers but the payload remains plain text or existing JSON shape.

Developer ergonomics and SDK API surface (concrete):
- JavaScript/TypeScript SDK: new field in request options: fidelity: {preset: "balanced" | "fast" | "authoritative" | custom: [{name, strategy}]}, toolTimeoutMs, attachmentMode.
- Python: streaming() helper yields frames that include .tier and .status properties. Helper apply_attachment(frame, attachment) provided.
- Provide a small migration helper on SDKs that auto-updates element ids and emits reconciliation logs for safety.

Pilot plan (8 weeks):
Week 0-1: finalize lattice wire encoding and lightweight frame flags (binary + header compatibility).
Week 2-3: implement server-side fallback scheduler and basic tool timeout plumbing (search connector + code-run connector).
Week 4: SDK prototypes for JS and Python (emit tier/status, apply_attachment helper).
Week 5-6: run pilot with 2 customers and internal teams (Console embeddings/assistants) with telemetry enabled.
Week 7: iterate on default presets and attachment_mode behaviors.
Week 8: ship v0 opt-in with docs and sample integration.

Risks and open questions:
- How to prevent user confusion when follow-up attachment replaces content already read? Need UX guidance for clients (toast/change highlight).
- Delta-attachments increase bandwidth; need to reason about billing model for follow-up attachments.
- Some tools (external APIs) are highly variable — deciding default budgets that work across regions is hard.
- Should we expose strict deadlines vs soft budgets? Current plan prefers soft budgets to avoid unnecessary cancellations.

Acceptance criteria for v0:
- Server emits tier/status metadata on frames and honors tool_timeout_hint in >=95% observed cases.
- SDKs expose fidelity primitives and demonstrate deterministic reconciliation with at least one pilot customer.
- Telemetry shows fallback reason breakdown and overall fallback rate <= 10% in pilot (configurable).

Next steps (action items):
- ENG: Spike on attaching stable element ids in frames and a low-cost follow-up event type (ENG-4021).
- PRODUCT: Draft developer docs and example flows for 3 sample apps (search-augmented chat, code-runner assistant, sales-research digest).
- DX: Prepare migration notes and example SDK snippets; plan a small tutorial.

Notes to reviewers:
- Looking for feedback on the lattice naming/semantics, whether attachment_mode is expressive enough, and whether we should add a "grace-synthesis" mode (server will hallucinate a minimal synthesized tool output flagged as synthesized).
